comment: Consent is not the universal governance mechanism for cross-border processing. Depending on the use case and legal framework, processing may be based on statutory healthcare functions, legal obligations or public-interest grounds, while individuals may exercise control through mechanisms such as access restrictions or opt-out rights. The EHDS expressly distinguishes these mechanisms. The Reference Architecture would therefore be more jurisdiction-neutral if it required implementers to establish the lawful basis and applicable individual-control model, rather than presuming a consent model.

public.text: Consent is not the universal governance mechanism for cross-border processing. Depending on the use case and legal framework, processing may be based on statutory healthcare functions, legal obligations or public-interest grounds, while individuals may exercise control through mechanisms such as access restrictions or opt-out rights. The EHDS expressly distinguishes these mechanisms. The Reference Architecture would therefore be more jurisdiction-neutral if it required implementers to establish the lawful basis and applicable individual-control model, rather than presuming a consent model.
public.suggestedRevision: Replace with: “The legal basis, applicable individual rights and control mechanisms, access-control rules and other data-governance arrangements for cross-border processing shall be explicit, including consent, restriction or opt-out mechanisms where applicable under the relevant legal framework.” Replace “consent considerations” with “health-specific legal, confidentiality, patient-rights and access-control requirements.”
